utterances.text: Now, at paragraphs 8 and 9 of your statement, it says that on the 11th of October, 1991, Milan Radojcic forced you to drive your minibus to transport JNA reservists. They were located at the outskirts of the town and you took them into the village. Would you be able to use a marker with the usher's assistance, please, to mark with an X the place where you picked up the reservists.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: I don't see the farm here. It is somewhere here in this part. A bit further up from the Borovo factory. It is the Lovas farm belonging to the agricultural combine of Lovas.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Do you see the Borovo factory in this picture?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: The Borovo factory and its perimeter are somewhere around here.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And approximately how far is the agricultural building that you said is not on the map, how far is that from the Borovo factory that you've just pointed out?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: The Borovo factory plot and the Lovas cooperative farm are adjacent to each other. They border on each other effectively.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Thank you. It appears that you've marked with a star, which is fine for my purposes. And the star marking, if you could confirm, indicates the place where you think the agricultural building is located. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: In the same paragraph of your statement, you said that the reservists set up check-points, including at the home of Jelena Antolovic. Can you mark her house with an A.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And what ethnicity was Jelena Antolovic?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: In paragraph 10 of your statement, it says that you took reservists from the agricultural building to the village centre three more times. Could you please use the marker to mark the other locations where you took the reservists with the letters B, C, and D.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: [Marks]. I don't see Mlinska Street anywhere here but it's somewhere around here, in this part here.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 10 of your statement you said that there was a tank at each location. Were there tanks stationed in other parts of Lovas?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Please indicate with --

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: Yes. At every check-point there was a tank, a lorry full of ammunition, and there were anti-armoured vehicles and APCs at various locations all around the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Mujic, were there tanks stationed in other places in Lovas or only at the check-points that you just marked for us?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: I saw the tanks only at the check-points, and as for the other vehicles that I mentioned, those were smaller-sized military vehicles, so-called transporters.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And do you know where these JNA reservists that you were transporting came from?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: From their conversation, I gained the impression that they were from Kragujevac, Valjevo, and other places in Serbia. I did not talk to them myself directly, but I heard what they were saying.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And after you transported these reservists and saw them establishing the check-points that you've marked on the map, did you believe that you were free to leave Lovas?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: No, I did not think that I was free to go anywhere from Lovas.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time the Prosecution would like to tender 65 ter 06276 as marked by the witness into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It shall be assigned Exhibit Number P297. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Next, Mr. Mujic, I'd like to ask you about what you saw during your work obligation which you've described at paragraph 14 of your statement. What neighbourhood of Lovas did you go to for your work obligation?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: As from the 12th of October, I was supposed to report every morning at 8.00 to the courtyard of the mechanical workshop of the Lovas agricultural cooperative in Kralja Tomislava Street. We all came there and that's where we were assigned work by Mr. Milan Radojcic and his assistant whose name I believe was Tepavac.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And where did they send you on these assignments?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: To various places. One day we went to the farm and we took out the engine from the combine and took it to the mill so they could use it to start the mill, and then one day we went to the farm of the PIK. That was a sort of youth operation. And we took metal beds apart and took them to Lovas to the building of -- where the municipality is now. One day we gathered mattresses, pillows, and blankets and took them to those same premises where the Dusan Silni Detachment would later go to sleep.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And other than these mattresses that you mentioned that were taken, what did you see happening to other Croat property in Lovas?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: I saw that various goods were used. They took items from garages. They took privately owned cars from garages, from yards. They used a blue lorry to transport household appliances. They would load these appliances onto the lorry and take them away.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And in paragraph 14 of your statement, you state that you saw a large double bus in Lovas with Novi Sad plates and that there were paramilitaries nearby. Who were these paramilitaries associated with?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: When I was passing down the street, I saw that in the yard there was a big bus, not a double-decker bus, but it was an articulated bus. We called it a Harmonika. It had Novi Sad registration plates, and given what they said, I understood that White Eagle members had come. They were Mirko Jovic's men from the Serbian Party of Renewal, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, for the next document I would like to move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: I would ask that 65 ter --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Hold on, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Mujic, how many men died from their injuries in the minefield?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: Twenty-one.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: I would like to ask the court officer to please bring up 65 ter 2226.1 and have that placed on the monitor before the witness. This is tab 5.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Mujic, have you seen this list before?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Do you agree that this is a list of persons who were killed in the minefield?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Those are the persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Mujic, when we met, you marked your initials "IM" in the left margin next to a number of the victims. What does this signify?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: It means that I saw these dead people with my very own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time we'd like to tender 65 ter 2226.1 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: We don't have an English translation of the list, Ms. Clanton?

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: We have an English translation of 2226 but not of the version that was marked by the witness. He marked it in his own language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. In -- Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: This document will be marked for identification until you upload the English translation of the other one --

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: -- with this one so that we have a translation of the text.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Mujic, I'm going -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It shall be assigned Exhibit Number P299, marked for identification. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Mujic, I'd like to briefly ask you a few questions about the medical treatment you've received. This is touched on in paragraph 44 of your statement. It says that you were sent to Sremska Mitrovica hospital in Serbia. What part of your body was operated on in Sremska Mitrovica hospital?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: My stomach because my intestines had been damaged as a result of the shrapnel.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And what was the ethnicity of the majority of the patients in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: They were mostly of Serbian ethnicity, or they were combatants from the front in Croatia. They had been wounded.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Other than the treatment that you received from your doctor, how were you treated by some of these other patients that had come from the front?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: If you could tell us, please, what kind of treatment you experienced from other patients or staff at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: The doctor and the staff treated me correctly, but the other patients, on some occasions they did establish contact with me but most of them didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And how would you characterize this contact?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: On one occasion a patient called Ivan Rusin addressed me, and he said that he had been wounded at the Vupik farm known as Ora. This was between Lovas and Sotina. His unit was present there -- or, rather, his unit had been mobilised as a -- Hungarians, Croats and so on as ethnic minorities, and they were sent to attack Vukovar, and they refused to do so, and they holed up in the farm, and JNA planes bombed them over a period of several days. So there were many persons who were killed and wounded. He lost his leg there and was wounded in the back by shrapnel.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Mujic, was your family able to visit you in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: No. Throughout that time period, I didn't see anyone from my family, neither my wife nor my children.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And was your doctor concerned about your well-being at this time?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was. He asked me on a number of occasions whether I had anyone, where my family members were. I said I didn't know where they were. I said that they had remained in Lovas and that I did not know whether they were still alive or not, and if they were alive, what sort of a situation they were in. He expressed his concern and said he would try to assist me. His name, the doctor's name was Nemanja Ljubisic. He is the surgeon who operated on me.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Was he concerned about what was going to happen to you?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: He was. At the end of my treatment, he said that pressure was being put on him to release me. So some people whom he did not name wanted to put me in a camp or a prison, that's what he said, and he said that he was concerned because my health was very poor, and he was afraid that some of the blows might harm me and that I might not survive such blows.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And do you know the name of the camp he was concerned you would be released to?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: He didn't mention a camp, really. He assumed that they would take me to Sremska Mitrovica to a prison or a camp, but they were always talking about some sort of a camp in the territory of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Where were you moved after you left the Sremska Mitrovica hospital?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: Dr. Ljubisic told me that he had arranged things. He asked a colleague of his in the rehabilitation centre in Stankamen to take me to some centre, to transfer me to some centre. So I think it was on the 1st or the 2nd of December that they found accommodation for me in the medical section together with Ivan Rusin and a combatant called Stevan Simic. So we were transferred to Stankamen.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Stari Slankamen.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Mujic, is Stari Slankamen a town in Serbia or in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: In Serbia, on the banks of the Danube.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And at Slankamen who did you see?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: When I was taken to Slankamen, they put me in a room. Several minutes later Zeljko Krnjaic entered the room. He is a Serb from Lovas and he was using crutches to walk.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And what did he say to you?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: When he entered the room, he immediately said: So it's you. If he was your brother, I killed him immediately, but I'll see what I'll do about you. I'll see what my kum will say about you. Milorad [as interpreted] Vorkapic, Silja, who is your former friend. Milan, not Milorad.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: He mentioned that if he were your brother, he would kill you. Did he talk about any other killings?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: He bragged that he had killed over 200 Ustasha, including Mato Sabljak from Lovas, whom he killed in the Tovarnik police station. He was very brazen. And he said that he killed him because Mato apparently had said once that the other would have to move from Lovas only because he was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Do you know why he confessed to you that he had committed these killings?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: He said that he could talk to me because I would not remain alive, and he said, If your former friend Silja Vorkapic says so, you will swim in the Danube, and he pointed to the river through the window.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Mujic, after you left Slankamen --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Clanton, before you move on, could you clarify what exactly this man said when entering the room, because it's not really clear on the record. He immediately said, "So it's you. He was your brother. I killed him immediately."

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Mujic, you've heard the Judge's comment. If you could clarify when Mr. Krnjaic came into the room exactly what he said to you.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: He recognised me, but he said, If it were your brother instead of you, I would kill him straight away. Given it was me and not my brother, he said he would see about me, what would happen to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Mujic, you've told us that when you returned to Lovas in December, you spent a very short time there. I believe it was three days. What did you think would happen to you if you stayed in Lovas?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: I knew I had to leave that hell as quickly as possible, because I didn't know who would come and what they would do to me after all I had been through.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Who was in charge in Lovas at this time?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: Paramilitary units like Dusan Silni and all sorts of volunteer groups. The number one person in the village was Ljuban Devetak with his assistants Milan Radojcic [Realtime transcript read in error "Rendulic"] and Milan Devcic who were his right-hand men.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: I'm aware of the time, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Excuse me. I notice a potential transcript problem. I'm not sure if the Prosecution wishes to correct it now or whether they will leave it to me, but in respect of one of the names that was just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Should we go into private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. It's not a private session issue. It's merely a name that may have been misrecorded or misstated.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. If I could please clarify with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Mujic, could you please give us the name of the person who was the assistant to Ljuban Devetak? I believe it was two names.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I mentioned Milan Radojcic, which was recorded as Rendulic, which is incorrect. And the other name that I mentioned was the name of Milan Devcic.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Thank you. I have two more questions, Your Honour, but I can pause now if you prefer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll take a break now. Mr. Witness, we'll take a break and come back at 12.45. The court usher will escort you out of the courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Clanton.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Mujic, before the break we were speaking about your ultimate departure from Lovas in 1991, and you stated that you were concerned what was going to happen to you and what people might do to you. Do you know what happened to some of the Croats who stayed in Lovas after you left?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Objection for the same reason that I interposed an objection earlier. There's no notice to my knowledge of this testimony in the witness summary or in the witness statement. Any such indication that there is is in the notice -- or the proofing note that was sent around last night extremely late. So I would object.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: The witness in his statement in paragraph 44 explains that he returned to Lovas after being away for several months and that he only stayed for about three days and he gives us information about the date of his departure. I'm only asking for him to give us any information he has that's relevant to the reason why he felt he had to leave and what he learned about the situation in Lovas at the time he felt he had to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have no objection to the first question, why he left. We would object to the second question, the second part of the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Objection overruled. Please proceed, Ms. Clanton.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Mujic, would you like for me to repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: You've told us that when you returned to Lovas, you were worried what was going to happen to you and what people might do to you. Do you know what happened to some of the Croats who stayed in Lovas after you left on December 16th?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was concerned because given what my wife had said, there were still paramilitary units in the area, and it would be best for us to leave. And therefore, on the 16th of December, my wife, my two children and I left and went to the free territory of Croatia. And while I was in hospital in Zagreb, I learned that during the period prior to Christmas, many crimes had been committed against Croats in Lovas. There was Madzarevic, Djuka Radocaj and so on, they were imprisoned in a cellar. They were maltreated. They drilled holes in their feet. They used pliers to extract their teeth. Madzarevic was badly beaten and he lost several teeth. They put salt on open wounds in his mouth. I learned about that because they were in the hospital in Zagreb and inhabitants of ours who were there visited them and myself. And it was in the conversation, in the course of conversations, that we came to learn about all of these things.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Mujic, these people who you've described, you've told us what happened to them and that you saw them when you were in Zagreb in the hospital. Do you know how it was that they left Lovas?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: They were beaten, and the local authorities moved them out en masse. There were a lot of women and children, and those beaten people, they forced them to sign some documents, and they moved them out and sent them away to the free territory of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: At this time, Your Honour, I have no further questions. There's one technical matter. During the break our Case Manager, Mr. Laugel, provided the English translation to the document that was MFI'd earlier. For the record, I would indicate that the B/C/S version has the annotations, the English does not, but if that could be admitted into evidence at this time, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: MFI status lifted. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: I apologise. Does it need to have an exhibit number at this time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It has one, hasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is Exhibit P299. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Good day to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: Good day to you as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: My name is Christopher Gosnell. I represent Mr. Hadzic in these proceedings, and I'll just be asking you a very few questions today. If anything is not clear, feel free to ask for a clarification. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, you were a driver in Lovas during these events, and you have a sense of some distances between places by road. Could you tell us how far it is from Lovas to Tovarnik by road approximately?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: About 7 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And how much further would it be from Tovarnik to the Serbian border by road?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: Not far. Perhaps 2 or 3 kilometres if not less than that. In any case, it's very close.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And leaving aside road distances, how far would it be as the crow flies from Lovas to the Serbian -- to the closest point where you could cross into Serbia?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: As the crow flies, of course it is much closer, but our agricultural fields are separated from the Serbian fields on the other side. I don't know how far or close it is, but I know that the distance is much shorter than if you were to go by road.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we have P297 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sir, this is the aerial image that you saw earlier and that you marked. From point B, is it possible to walk south towards Serbia and to reach the border?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: It is possible. There is a dirt road there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And how far would that be from point B to the Serbian border?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: I really can't say. I was never a farmer. I never -- or seldom took that road, but I don't think it's far.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Would you agree that it would be about 3 kilometres?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: Possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sir, yesterday during your conversations with the Office of the Prosecutor you indicated to them that there was a ZNG unit based in the old school building in Lovas at some point; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Can you tell us when that unit arrived?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date, but it was sometime during the summer, perhaps in July or August, but they did not stay long. They stayed for a very short while.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Approximately how many men were part of this unit?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: I believe that they were the size of a squad, up to 30 men, or a platoon, rather. I was never inside their premises. I never counted them, but that's how I remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: But did you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell, could you ask the witness for a year, July or August?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. Witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And did you ever see members of this unit outside of where they were staying at the old school building?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Do you have any indication or knowledge as to their activities while they were in Lovas?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: I did not monitor those activities. I didn't know anything about them. They were billeted there. They were there during the day. I don't know whether they went somewhere during the day or at any time. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did they ever assist you with the check-points that you say in your statement you participated in manning?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did man the check-points, and they never participated in those check-points, only our locals were there, and they had hunting rifles as weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: You never saw any members of this unit engaging in patrols around the town?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: Well, they did walk around the village. They would go to the local cafe. They would be here and there, but I never saw them patrolling.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Is it your testimony that you never saw them outside of the old Zadruga building with their weapons?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: As I've already told you, they would go to the cafe. They did go through the village, but they did not act in an organised fashion. It is possible that some of them were carrying weapons when they did that, but I can't tell you that for a fact. I can't tell you that I saw them or who I saw doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I have to correct my last question, Mr. President. It was the old school building, not the old Zadruga building. Sir, did you see these individuals wearing uniforms?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's the guys that I'm talking about. They were billeted in the old school, and I did see them wearing uniforms. They -- they did have their personal weapons, but I did not see them acting in an organised manner doing anything in the village. I did them -- did see them going to the cafe as individuals, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: When you say "personal weapons," are you referring to -- well, what are you referring to when you say "personal weapons"? What kind of weapons?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: As far as I could see, they had rifles, semi-automatic and automatic rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And you never spoke to any of these individuals?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: I did. Of course I did. There were several of them who were locals who were members of those units. I knew them, and I did talk to them, but I was never part of that unit, so we did not actually discuss the unit matter -- matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: You say some of the individuals were local. Am I correct in understanding that some of them were not local?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Some of them were not locals, but I don't know those men, so I can't say anything about those men who were not locals.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, did the people you do know or did know who were in the unit, did they tell you anything about who these non-locals were?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did the people you did know who were in the unit tell you that weapons had been brought to Lovas as part of the establishment of this unit there?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: No. I didn't have anything to do with them. They came. They brought their weapons, and then when they left, they took the weapons away with them. I don't know what else to tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did anyone to your knowledge from the Crisis Committee ask that they participate in manning roadblocks or otherwise defending the town?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: I know nothing about that, because I was not a member of the inner circle of the Crisis Staff. Therefore, I was not privy to any such decisions, if there were any such decisions, nor could I take part in the passing of such decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And when did this unit leave Lovas?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: I don't know the date. I believe that it was still summer. It may have been in the month of August perhaps, but I don't know. I really did not pay much attention to that at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, are you sure that they weren't there in September?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: I don't think so, because in the month of September we could not leave the village. So I don't think that they were in the village in the month of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: But there was a build-up of Serb forces around or near Lovas in August and September; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I heard about that. On several occasions Lovas was attacked or, rather, it was targeted by cannon shells. I don't know what kind of shells those were, but the village was shelled several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Was there any shooting in addition to shelling from the Serb side or was it just shelling?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: Just shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And you're saying that this unit left just as this shelling begins. Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: No. I think that they left the village even before the shelling. I can't be a hundred per cent sure, but that's what I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: At paragraph 3 of your statement - and you can look at it there in front of you, sir, if you wish - you say that there was a -- a gradual build-up, military presence and artillery, "and we were aware that the village of Sotin had been attacked. There was also a demand from the JNA to surrender all weapons, but there was nothing to surrender." Can you tell us when this demand to surrender weapons was made by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: That happened on several occasions. Our representatives, together with some other local Serbs, went to attend the negotiations. I don't know when those negotiations started, but there were several rounds of them. I don't know when it was -- or, rather, I don't remember when those negotiations were taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Were these negotiations taking place at the same time that there were check-points being manned by Croats in the village?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Croats manned check-points at entrances and exits from the village all the -- all the time up to the 10th of October. A few days before the 10th of October, they stopped manning those check-points.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So you're saying that the check-points were in existence right up until the time of the Serb attack; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: A few days prior to the 10th of October those check-points were dismantled and disbanded, because the JNA and the Serb forces insisted that we should surrender our weapons. We hesitated. Some wanted to surrender the -- the hunting rifles that we had. Some were against that. So we simply stopped manning the check-points because we knew that it was just a matter of days when the village would be -- be attacked. We did not have the necessary power to defend ourselves, so the village was simply left at the mercy of the powers that be.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: During the negotiations with the JNA, if that was the view of the Croat side, did you or representatives of the Crisis Committee invite the JNA into the village?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: No. Nobody invited them to come to the village. In view of all the developments, we realised and we were certain that the JNA was no longer our military, that they sided up with the Serbs and that they were no longer our friends, that they did not come to protect our people.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did you indicate that the check-points that were being manned had been dismantled? Was that conveyed to the JNA?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether they learnt about it. We never informed them. We tried to deal with our own problems. We tried to see how we would save our women and children and frail and elderly. We tried to see how we would save ourselves. That was our main preoccupation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And in doing that, in protecting yourselves and the women and children, isn't it true that you tried to maintain control of Lovas for as long as possible?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: Well, it was only normal, but we simply lost steam. Lovas had been encircled for a long time. We did not have electricity. We were simply forced to look -- look after number one, to look after our own families. We were under a lot of pressure.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Were any white flags raised above the town before the attack by the JNA on Lovas?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: No. White flags and bands around our arms, that was ordered to us by those who entered the village on the 10th of October. So all Croatian houses had to put a white sheet on their gates, and the Croats at the same time were ordered to mark their sleeves with a white band as a sign of recognition.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sir, my question was -- about the white flags was related to whether or not there were any visible indications given by the townspeople of Lovas that they were surrendering to the JNA. Were there any such indications given by members of the town -- by the inhabitants of Lovas to that effect?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, no such thing happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, you say in your statement at paragraph 6 that -- and this is describing when you emerge from the basement that you have taken refuge in, and you say --

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: You say: "Outside on the road, I saw a person in the uniform of a JNA captain together with a man named Milan Radojcic, who was also wearing the uniform of a JNA captain and was holding a handgun. I was very surprised to see this, because Radojcic was a Serb from the village of Lovas with a house there." And then you say: "As far as I was aware, his uniform was regular JNA and not reservist." Now, my first question is: Do you know whether there are any differences between a JNA reserve uniform and a JNA active-duty uniform? Is there a difference?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: Before all of those developments, at one point in time I was a reservist myself, a member of the JNA reserve. I had been issued with an olive-drab JNA uniform, the thicker kind. On the 11th, around noon, Milan Radojcic came into the courtyard of a neighbouring house. That house belonged to Anka Krizmanic, and we heard a shot, and somebody was crying out, Is there anybody there --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sir, excuse me, can I just cut you off.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I was just for the moment interested in whether or not you know whether there is any difference between a reserve uniform of the JNA and a regular active-duty uniform of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: I think that an active-duty uniform is made of somewhat better material, somewhat thinner material. He was in a shirt, and he had three stars on his epaulettes, and I knew that that represented the rank of a captain.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, could a reserve officer have a rank of captain and have three stars on their epaulette?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I know that a JNA captain was discerned by the three epaulettes -- the three stars on the epaulette. That's all I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, all I'm getting at, sir, is just to try to understand what your basis was for believing at the time that he was an active member of the JNA instead of -- instead of a reserve member of the JNA. Was it on the basis of his uniform?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: Yes. And I found it strange that he was a captain, be it a reserve or an active-duty officer. I saw those men wearing all sorts of different uniforms or parts of uniforms. So at first -- my first thought was to wonder how come that he was a JNA captain, because I knew him personally. He was a Lovas local. We always had a very good relationship before those developments.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So you don't know whether he was active duty or reserve at this time. Is that a fair conclusion to your testimony on this?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: Well, one could say so, but it's true that he had three stars and the rank of a captain. That is true. As to whether he was a reserve officer or an active-duty officer, I'm not sure whether that is all that important now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: At paragraph 8 of your statement, you say -- you describe being directed by this Montenegrin captain who was in the JNA, that he directed you towards an agricultural field on the outside of the village and opened the door of a store where there were many reservists inside. I just want to make it absolutely clear, because it's not clear from the statement. These are JNA reservists; correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And at paragraph 10, you stay you returned to this field three times, and you took them to various locations in the village where they set up check-points to prevent people entering or leaving. Is it correct to say that you understood that the JNA was controlling the perimeter of Lovas at this point?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was my impression. When I was driving them around, the impression I gained was that they were carrying out checks, providing security at the entrance and exit to -- from the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So they were checking those who came in and they were checking those who went out; correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And in particular, they were controlling a check-point on the road leading south to Tovarnik; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Was there a tank at that particular check-point?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And that was the case throughout the time that you were in Lovas; correct? Until you left on the 18th.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Was that the case when you returned in December?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: I didn't notice it then. I returned home. I didn't go anywhere until I left on the 16th again, until I left the village. All I know is that when I was driven to an area behind the village, by the farm at the exit from the village, there was a check-point, but I didn't see who was manning it. I didn't see their insignia, their uniforms or anything like that because I just passed by.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: At paragraph 30 of your statement, which is at page 6 of the English, but you can refer to the numbers -- the paragraph numbers there in front of you, you have just finished describing these terrible events at -- where the beatings occur in the yard of the Zadruga building, as I understand it.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And you say here at paragraph 30: "Milan Rendulic (Buva), a Croat, and Ilija Kresojevic, a Serb," appear to arrive there. And then you say: "They ordered the group that I was in to get into pairs in a line and we were immediately flanked either side by this special unit." Just again to make your statement absolutely clear, when you say "by this special unit," do I understand that the special unit you're referring to is the special unit you describe in the paragraph before, paragraph 29? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And why was a Croat involved in participating on the Serbian side when he arrived there?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: He wasn't involved. It was his choice. His wife was a Serb, Koviljka Japundzic, and his brother-in-law was Milan Devcic -- rather, his son-in-law was Milan Devcic, who was the chief of police in SAO Krajina, in Lovas. So he sided with -- with them probably because he cared about these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Were there any other Croats that you knew of who were fighting on the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't notice any such cases. I didn't say he was fighting on the Serbian side, but he somehow joined them and took action with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, do you know what unit he was a member of?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't know anything about that. He and Ilija Kresojevic entered the yard of the workshop. They were wearing the uniforms of the reserve JNA force. Naturally they had semi-automatic rifles that they had slung over their shoulders.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So you say that they were wearing the uniforms of the reserve JNA force. Did he have any markings to indicate his rank?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: No. I didn't notice any such markings.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: At paragraph 42 of your statement, which is page 7 of the English, you say that you managed to get onto the road and a truck being driven by Milan Vorkapic arrived, "and we were put on board the truck and taken firstly to Tovarnik and then to Sid where we had to wait for some sort of medical treatment."

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Do you remember whether the truck you were on was accompanied by any other vehicle?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: What was the vehicle and who was inside?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: It was a privately owned vehicle that they had taken from Milko Keser. It was a Zastava 124, a red one, I believe, and there were two members of the paramilitary unit, or Chetniks, as we would say. They were armed. And Milan Vorkapic, also known as Trnda, was driving the lorry and they were escorting us. They drove behind the lorry and they did so as far as Sid.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: You say paramilitary unit or Chetniks. Do you know which unit -- what unit specifically are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know, because I heard nothing about that. The village was full of those units, and we didn't know whether they were military units or paramilitary units. Their insignia were of different kinds. They had mixed uniforms, parts of uniforms, so the markings on their caps were also different, and therefore we didn't know which units they belonged to. And in addition, our position was such that we didn't even dare look anyone in the eye in order to avoid beatings, let alone look at someone in order to try and determine which unit that person was a member of.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could these people have been members of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And as you were driving between Tovarnik and Sid, did you stop at the border with Serbia?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: We only stopped in Tovarnik, somewhere in the centre. They opened the rear end of the lorry. I saw someone in a white overall appear, and I think there was a nurse with him --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sorry, sir, to just focus you. I'm not so interested in what happened in Tovarnik because that's already in your statement. The question is whether between Tovarnik and Sid you stopped at any check-point at the Serbian border --

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure, but I wouldn't say so, but I don't know. We were concerned with ourselves. We were all wounded. I had been seriously wounded. So there's some details that I haven't remembered even if I saw them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: That's completely understandable, sir. And on the return -- on the return trip from Sid to Lovas, do you remember whether you stopped at the border?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: I don't think so, but again I'm not certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And at any other time that you took that road between Tovarnik and Sid -- well, first of all, did you ever take that road at any other time, let's say before October 10th, between Tovarnik and Sid?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: When --

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: No, no. I took that road on the 21st of September when Tovarnik was attacked or, rather, shelled, and on that occasion I drove the bus to Tovarnik in order to fetch children, women, and the elderly who were afraid as a result of that shelling. So on that day I went to collect several elderly persons, women and children, and bring them back. That was the last time I was in Tovarnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: When you were evacuated for medical treatment to Sremska Mitrovica, did you travel by that road from Tovarnik to Sid and then into Serbia?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Do you recall on that occasion whether there was a check-point at the border that you had to stop at?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: I think there were check-points, but I don't think we stopped because it was a medical vehicle that was being used to drive us to our destination.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And when you returned to Lovas in December, did you go via Sid and Tovarnik?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: On that occasion, did you have to go through a border post or a check-point between the Serbian and Croat side?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And what did you observe there at that time?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: Well, there was a check-point. You had to show certain documents, passes, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And as far as you could tell, who was in charge of that post or check-point?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: I don't know who controlled the check-point. I didn't even notice this because I was very afraid, so I wasn't really paying attention, so I could not say.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, when you went to the hospital in Sremska Mitrovica, do you know the name of the hospital, the exact name of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Just waiting for a translation.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Was it a military or a civilian hospital?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: I think it was a civilian hospital. I was in the surgical ward, and I was operated on that very same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And during your stay at this hospital, you have described having a conversation with someone of either Hungarian or Croatian ethnic extraction, and you say that they told you that they had been sent to attack Vukovar and that they had holed up in a farm. This is at page 61 of today's transcript. They were holed up in a farm and that JNA planes bombed them over a period of several days. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did you believe that story?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: It's not that I believed it. I knew when these planes bombed that area. We heard about that, or we heard it because it was in the vicinity. It was close to our place. The planes made a lot of noise, and there were these very forceful explosions, but we knew that there was a unit there, because several days earlier they came to our farm in order to get some drinking water.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And was it at that time that you learned that this was a unit composed of Croats and Hungarians?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that at the time. I found out about that in the hospital. This wounded person whose name is Ivan Rusin told me about that. He told me that they were supposed to launch an attack on Vukovar but their commander didn't want to do so and they sent the planes in to bomb them. That's true because I know about this bombing because later, after the event, some of us were curious so we went there by motorbike and saw that everything had been bombed. There was a lot of blood, and that gentleman told me that according to his information, there were quite a few men who had been killed and a lot of men who had been wounded there, and they had been taken to hospitals throughout Vojvodina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So you're saying that what happened was that this unit mutinied and refused orders to attack or participate in the attack on Vukovar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: According to what this gentleman in Mitrovica said, yes, that is correct, and I believe what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: All right. So you heard about the mutiny part from him, but you did yourself see or were aware of the bombing of the unit; correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I knew about it. We all heard -- heard it, and later, once they had all fled, we saw that there had been a lot of bombing at that place, and there were a lot of -- there was a lot of residential housing that had been destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So had this unit comprised of Croats and Hungarians taken residence in these residential houses? Is that where they had taken refuge?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: They had found accommodation there. As to where they were sleeping and who exactly, I don't know, but they stayed there for a certain period of time until these planes of theirs attacked them, because the Vupik, the agricultural unit, had accommodation there for seasonal workers. So there was accommodation that was available.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: You said earlier today -- or you described to us earlier today your discussion with a Zeljko Krnjaic. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And you say that he bragged about killing 200, and this is in quotation marks, "200 Ustasha," and --

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And the word you used in your testimony earlier today at page 63 was that he was bragging. Do you -- did you believe the story that he had killed 200 Ustasha?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: Well, I believed it, because knowing them -- and it wasn't just in Lovas. They probably waged war in other battle-fields. And on the 10th of October they entered Lovas and they killed people in their houses and in the streets, and therefore, since I knew that that was the case, I thought that anything was possible. Because Krnjaic, on the 10th of October, entered Lovas, and 22 locals from Lovas were killed on that day for no reason. This was done in the houses, in the yards, in the streets, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And what unit was he a member of?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't pay attention to that. I don't have any information about that. They were all members of some sort of units, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And you met him in this rehabilitation centre in Serbia when he told you this story; correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And who -- who were the patients at this rehabilitation centre?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. On the whole there were combatants from the Serbian side. There were civilians as well. So I don't have any information. Since on the first day when I arrived there, ten minutes passed and he entered my room then, and when he told me what he did on that day and on the following day, well, in my opinion a lot of terrible things happened. I was transferred to another room, and unknown individuals came to see me. They were wearing white clothes. They threatened me. They were wearing white overalls. They threatened me. They said I was their patient and that I would not survive. So I was very scared. And afterwards, sometime later, the duty doctor in that ward came to see me and to examine me, and she noticed that I was very scared, and she only asked me whether anyone had come to see me. I no longer had any reason to remain silent. I said yes, and I told her everything. And she told me to wait a while, and she said that she was going to see her boss.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. Mujic, thank you very much for your testimony. Your Honours, I have no further questions. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Any redirect?

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Mujic, a moment ago Defence counsel asked you about this unit that you were aware of that was made up of minorities, Hungarians and Croats. What kind of unit was this?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: It was a unit that had been mobilised. It consisted of the reserve forces of the JNA and they were from Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And can you tell us the name of the area they were accommodated?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: It was at the Vupik farm, the agricultural complex. That's where they had been provided with accommodation. That's where there were machines for agricultural work. There were the workshops, the offices, and there was accommodation there for seasonal workers as well. At one point in time, I can't remember the year, perhaps it was after 1980, there was a youth action in the former Yugoslavia, a youth work action, and there were quite a lot of facilities for accommodation as a result. So the beds, et cetera, remained in Vupik. And one day after Lovas had been occupied, we were taken there so that we could take some of the beds --

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Mujic, if I could ask you --

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: -- to the premises of the local commune --

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: If I could ask you to stop there, please. This Vupik farm that you've described, is this close to the village of Lovas?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: It's between Lovas and Sutina. It's perhaps 5 kilometres from Lovas. By the road. By the Tovarnik-Lovas-Sutina road.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And do you recall what month the accommodation -- this facility was shelled? Or bombed?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUJIC
utterances.text: It was sometime towards the end of September.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, this brings an end to your testimony. We thank you for coming to The Hague to assist the Tribunal. You're now released as a witness. The court usher will escort you out of court, and we wish you a safe journey back home. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Clanton, the Bench's secret services informed me that this was your very first witness examination in court. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Well, we certainly wouldn't have noticed if we hadn't been told. Congratulations, Ms. Clanton.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Is there anything else for the moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. We notice that there is a few minutes left in the session, but given the time, we actually had the next witness sent back to the hotel. So if we could start tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Nothing else to be addressed, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
